Heritage sites by state

Heritage sites in Kerala: Kochi, Muziris and temple towns

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Kerala's heritage is shaped by the sea and the monsoon. Key sites include Fort Kochi and Mattancherry, the Muziris project area around Kodungallur and Pattanam, the Edakkal cave engravings, Padmanabhapuram Palace, Bekal Fort, Kerala temple towns such as Thrissur, and living arts such as Koodiyattam. Its only World Heritage listing is the Western Ghats.

We design study tours to Kochi, Muziris, Thrissur and Edakkal for groups on request.

Why Kerala's heritage is different

Kerala looks west to the Arabian Sea, and for over two thousand years its history has been tied to ocean trade in pepper, cardamom and other spices. Roman, Arab, Chinese, Jewish, Portuguese, Dutch and British traders all came, and several communities settled for good: Syrian Christians, Jews of Kochi, Mappila Muslims. The Chera kings of the early period, the later Chera rulers of Mahodayapuram, the Zamorins of Kozhikode, the rajas of Kochi and the kings of Travancore built the political frame.

Kerala's building tradition is also distinct: sloping tiled or copper roofs, timber frames and laterite walls designed for heavy rain. Even its temples look different from the stone towers of Tamil Nadu. Our lecture on sacred architecture across communities compares Kerala's temples, churches, mosques and synagogues, which share much of this building language.

Heritage walks in this state: Kochi

Museums in Kerala

  • Napier Museum, Thiruvananthapuram. Bronzes, ivory and art in a 19th-century building.
  • Hill Palace Museum, Tripunithura. Former Kochi royal palace with collections of the rajas.
  • Pazhassi Raja Archaeological Museum, Kozhikode. Megalithic finds, coins and sculpture.
  • Kerala Folklore Museum, Kochi. Masks, costumes and objects of performing traditions.

UNESCO in Kerala: the Western Ghats and Koodiyattam

Kerala has no cultural World Heritage Site. Its listed property is part of the Western Ghats serial natural site (2012), including Periyar, Silent Valley, Eravikulam and other forest areas. Separately, Koodiyattam, Sanskrit theatre performed in temple theatres (koothambalams), and Mudiyettu, a ritual dance drama, are on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. That is a different list from World Heritage Sites; our explainer on intangible cultural heritage explains the difference.

Archaeological sites in Kerala

The Edakkal caves, in Wayanad, are a natural rock shelter formed by a split boulder. Their walls carry engraved human figures, animals and symbols, usually considered prehistoric to early historic, and a few short later inscriptions. Our rock art of India session places Edakkal in the wider Indian picture.

Muziris, the ancient port named in Tamil Sangam poems and Roman sources, has long been sought near Kodungallur. Excavations at Pattanam since 2007 found Roman amphora pieces, beads and other trade goods, and many archaeologists see it as part of the Muziris port area, though the identification is still discussed. The Muziris Heritage Project links Pattanam with the Paliam palace, the Cheraman Juma Masjid (rebuilt in later centuries, with traditions linking it to early Islam in Kerala) and other sites around Kodungallur. Our session on foods as historical evidence uses pepper and coconut to tell this trade story.

Megalithic burials, including rock-cut caves, hood stones (kudakkal) and hat stones (topikallu), are found across the state; Porkulam and Cheramangad near Thrissur are known groups.

Ancient temples and churches in Kerala

The Vadakkunnathan temple in Thrissur, set within a large walled compound, is a classic Kerala temple, with circular and square shrines under tiered roofs and murals, and is the setting for the Thrissur Pooram festival. The Padmanabhaswamy temple in Thiruvananthapuram, rebuilt in the 18th century under Marthanda Varma of Travancore, has a gopuram in the Tamil style. Kerala murals of the 16th to 18th centuries survive at Ettumanoor, Vaikom and the Mattancherry palace.

Kerala has some of India's oldest Christian communities. Churches such as those at Kuravilangad and Kottayam (the Valiyapalli, with Persian crosses) show Syrian Christian traditions. St Francis Church in Fort Kochi, built by the Portuguese in the early 16th century, is where Vasco da Gama was first buried. The Paradesi Synagogue in Mattancherry dates to 1568.

Forts, palaces and colonial Kochi

Padmanabhapuram Palace, the old Travancore palace, is now in Tamil Nadu's Kanyakumari district but is run by Kerala. It is the finest surviving example of Kerala timber palace architecture. Bekal Fort, in Kasaragod, is a large laterite fort of the 17th century on the sea. Thalassery Fort was built by the English East India Company, and St Angelo Fort at Kannur by the Portuguese in 1505.

Fort Kochi and Mattancherry together show Portuguese, Dutch and British layers, the Jewish quarter, spice warehouses and the Mattancherry (Dutch) Palace with its murals. Our heritage walk in Kochi guide covers the route.

Living arts and crafts of Kerala

Much of Kerala's heritage is performed. Kathakali, the dance drama with painted faces and huge skirts, developed in the 17th century, and Mohiniyattam is the state's classical solo dance. Theyyam, in the north, is a ritual form in which performers become deities for a night in village shrines and sacred groves (kavus). Koodiyattam is performed in temple theatres, and Kalaripayattu is a martial tradition taught in special training halls. Our lecture on martial arts and society puts Kalaripayattu in historical context.

Crafts tie closely to trade and to the temple economy: bell metal at Kunjimangalam, Aranmula metal mirrors (which have a Geographical Indication tag), coir, and the timber skills of house and boat builders. The uru, the large wooden boat built at Beypore near Kozhikode, continues a shipbuilding tradition linked to Arabian Sea trade. Snake boats and the boat races of Alappuzha are living descendants of riverine warfare and festival culture.

Groups should treat Theyyam and temple festivals as worship, not shows. Ask before photographing, follow the dress rules of each shrine, and stay with local guides who know the customs.

Planning a heritage trip in Kerala

Kochi is the base for Fort Kochi, Mattancherry, the Muziris area and Thrissur. Thiruvananthapuram covers Padmanabhapuram and the museums. Wayanad covers Edakkal; the north (Kannur, Thalassery, Bekal) is a separate leg. The monsoon is beautiful but heavy; October to March is easier. Non-Hindus are not allowed into many Kerala temples, so check before planning. Check the ASI or state archaeology website for timings.

Kerala visits are planned around your group. We design a study tour for your group and private journeys, with a lecture first.

Questions people ask

Are there any UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Kerala?

Kerala shares the Western Ghats natural serial site (2012), with components such as Periyar and Silent Valley. It has no cultural World Heritage Site. Koodiyattam and Mudiyettu are on UNESCO's separate intangible heritage list.

What is special about the Edakkal caves?

Edakkal in Wayanad is a natural rock shelter whose walls carry engraved human and animal figures and symbols, usually considered prehistoric to early historic, with a few later inscriptions. It is one of south India's best known rock art sites.

Where was the ancient port of Muziris?

Muziris is usually placed near Kodungallur. Excavations at Pattanam, nearby, found Roman amphorae, beads and other trade goods, and many archaeologists link it to the Muziris port area, though the identification is still debated.

Can Talaash Heritage plan a Kerala study tour?

Yes, on request. We design study tours for schools, colleges and adult groups, for example Kochi, the Muziris sites and Thrissur, and can add a lecture on Indian Ocean trade or sacred architecture before you travel.
